result.summary: Pindar opens a short victory ode for the boxer Agesidamos of Epizephyrian Lokris, who won at Olympia in 484 B.C. He says songs are due to winners, promises a fuller ode for the celebration in Italy, and praises the Lokrians as cultured and brave.

scenes.title: Editor's introductory note
scenes.summary: A note explains that this ode was sung at Olympia on the night of the victory and that a longer ode is promised. It dates the victory to 484 B.C.

scenes.title: Pindar promises a song of triumph
scenes.summary: Pindar says that songs are owed to winners and promises Agesidamos a song of praise. He asks the Muses to join in and to visit the Lokrians, a people of arts and arms.
scenes.stakes: Pindar has a debt of praise to pay; the poet's promise to the victor must be kept.

characters.name: Pindar

notable_quotes.reason: A memorable proverb that inborn character cannot be changed, used here to praise the Lokrians' nature.

analysis.text: The ode treats praise-song as a debt owed to success won through labour, and links excellence to divine help.
Olympic victory odes were commissioned by victors or their cities. Here the ode is sung at Olympia on the night of the victory, with a longer one promised for the celebration at home.

language_notes.text: The 'longer one' is Olympian 11, written for Agesidamos' celebration at Epizephyrian Lokris in southern Italy, so the 'Italian home' means the Lokrian colony there.
The 'prelude' and 'pledge confirmed by oath' mean this short song is a first instalment, promising a fuller ode later.
'Fain' means eager or glad; 'to keep some part in fold' continues the shepherd image of storing glory as in a sheepfold.
'Stranger-banishing' describes a people who expel foreigners; Pindar says the Lokrians are the opposite, hospitable and cultured.
Fox and lion stand for inborn character. Lokrian nature, like theirs, cannot change, so the praise of their arts and arms holds.

context_notes.text: Agesidamos won the boys' boxing at Olympia. The victor's crown there was a wreath of wild olive.
The Muses are the goddesses of poetry, music and the arts, here invited to join the victory song.

literary_notes.text: Winds and rain stand for the different needs of life; the opening gnomic image leads to the point that victory calls for song.
Pindar calls himself a shepherd who folds part of the glory in his song, treating praise as a flock he tends.
Pindar turns to address the Muses directly, asking them to come to the Lokrians and join the victory song.
Animal examples serve as a comparison for inborn Lokrian character, grounding the praise in nature.
